subject: Medicine
summary: Intestinal obstruction is a blockage of the bowel that stops normal passage of contents. It can be mechanical or functional, and requires prompt assessment to prevent ischemia and perforation.

sections.p: Intestinal obstruction is a complete or partial blockage of the intestinal lumen, preventing passage of food, fluid, and gas. Diagnosis combines history, physical exam, and imaging, with plain abdominal X‑ray or ultrasound as first steps.

t.b: Shows dilated loops and air‑fluid levels; confirms mechanical obstruction.

sections.p: Severity is staged by the presence of strangulation, perforation, or peritonitis. The Bell staging system (I–III) is commonly used: I—non‑complicated obstruction; II—complicated without peritonitis; III—peritonitis or perforation.

In low‑resource settings, the top causes are adhesions, hernias, and intestinal parasites such as Ascaris lumbricoides and hookworm. Other common causes include volvulus, intussusception in children, and tumors.
Patients present with crampy abdominal pain, vomiting (often bilious), distension, and obstipation. Visible peristalsis is a classic sign of obstruction but not of peritonitis.
Investigations aim to confirm obstruction, identify the level, and detect complications. When advanced imaging is unavailable, clinical judgment and basic imaging guide management.

sections.p: Urgent red flags include sudden severe pain, peritonitis signs, high lactate, or hemodynamic instability. Complications are ischemia, perforation, sepsis, and electrolyte disturbances.

Treat the underlying cause first (e.g., hernia repair, parasite eradication). Provide supportive care: nasogastric decompression, IV fluids, electrolyte correction, and broad‑spectrum antibiotics if perforation is suspected.

sections.p: After resolution, monitor for recurrence, nutritional status, and underlying risk factors. Prevention focuses on early hernia repair, anti‑helminthic treatment, and safe surgical practices.

t.b: Identify malnutrition that may delay healing.

sections.p: Intestinal obstruction is often mistaken for gastroenteritis, functional constipation, or abdominal migraine. Distinguishing features include visible peristalsis, vomiting, and imaging findings.

sections.p: Plain X‑ray may appear normal in early obstruction; normal lactate does not rule out ischemia if taken early. Clinical signs can be subtle in children or the elderly.

faq.q: Can intestinal obstruction be caused by parasites?
faq.a: Yes, heavy Ascaris or hookworm infections can block the bowel, especially in children.

faq.q: What is the most common cause in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Hernias and intestinal parasites are the leading causes.
Only mechanical obstructions that do not resolve with conservative care or that are complicated require surgery.
